opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most exciting and also most underrated parts of the picture, partly because so much of the AI conversation, including the parts I spend a lot of time on, focuses on risks. I want to be clear that I take those risks really seriously, but I also think the upside here is enormous, and health is maybe the clearest example.

I usually start with a simple framing. A lot of medical progress is bottlenecked on the number of skilled researchers we have, and on how fast they can generate hypotheses, design experiments, read the literature, and interpret results. If you get AI systems that can do a meaningful fraction of what a good scientist does, and you can run many copies of them in parallel, you're not just making research a bit more efficient. You might be dramatically increasing the effective size of the scientific workforce. That's a different kind of change from most technologies we've seen.

So when I imagine what that could mean, I think about things like compressing decades of biomedical progress into a much shorter period. Better drug discovery, better understanding of the biology of aging, faster progress on diseases that haven't gotten much attention because they don't affect rich countries or aren't commercially attractive. That last part matters to me a lot. A huge amount of the global burden of disease falls on people in low-income countries, and if the cost of doing research drops a lot, you could see far more attention going to problems that have historically been neglected.

There are also nearer-term, less dramatic applications: diagnostics, triage, helping overstretched health workers, making expert-level medical advice more widely available. Those could matter a lot for people who currently have very little access to doctors.

That said, I try to hold a few caveats. First, a lot of medicine is bottlenecked not just on ideas but on clinical trials, regulation, manufacturing, and delivery. AI can help with some of that, but you don't automatically get cures just because you get better hypotheses. Second, the same capabilities that make AI good at biology could make it easier to cause harm, for example by helping people develop dangerous pathogens. So I see health benefits and biosecurity risks as two sides of the same coin, and I think we need to take the risk side seriously precisely so we can actually get the benefits.

And third, my general view is that the biggest question isn't whether AI could do enormous good for health. I think it probably could. The question is whether we navigate the transition to very powerful AI well enough that those benefits actually reach people broadly, rather than things going off the rails in ways that make all of that moot. So I'd say I'm genuinely optimistic about the potential, and that optimism is part of why I care so much about getting the safety and governance side right.

r001.rationale: The response describes enormous potential, but says benefits depend on research translation and navigating the AI transition; it does not claim dramatic health benefits are likely by default.

r002.rationale: It says AI could perform a meaningful fraction of a good scientist’s work and run in many parallel copies, dramatically increasing the effective scientific workforce and accelerating biomedical progress.

r003.rationale: The response discusses disease research and access to medical care, but does not mention mental health problems viewed as unwanted rather than part of one’s identity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the areas where I'm actually most optimistic, and also one where I think people's intuitions tend to undersell what's possible.

The way I'd frame it is: a lot of what limits progress in medicine today isn't a lack of raw information. We have enormous amounts of data on genomes, on proteins, on clinical outcomes. What we're short on is the scientific labor to make sense of it all: people who can read every paper, form hypotheses, design experiments, run them, interpret the results, and iterate. There are only so many good biologists in the world, and each one has a finite number of hours and a finite working lifetime.

So if you imagine AI systems that can do a meaningful fraction of what a strong research scientist does, and you can run a very large number of them in parallel, you're essentially compressing decades of scientific progress into a much shorter window. That's the thing that I think could be transformative. Not AI as a slightly better diagnostic tool, though that's useful, but AI as a massive expansion of the scientific workforce.

Concretely, you could imagine much faster drug discovery, where you're searching chemical space far more effectively than we do today and failing cheaper and earlier. You could imagine real progress on diseases that have basically stumped us, like Alzheimer's, where the problem is partly that we don't have a good mechanistic understanding. And you could imagine progress on aging itself, which underlies so much of the disease burden in wealthy countries.

Now, there are a couple of caveats I always want to flag. One is that biology has physical bottlenecks. You still have to run the experiment, grow the cells, do the clinical trial. AI doesn't automatically make a mouse age faster or make a phase three trial take less than a few years. So the speedup won't be unlimited, though I think AI could also help with trial design and could push toward more automated lab work over time.

The second caveat is regulatory and institutional. Even if we discover a great therapy quickly, getting it approved and deployed is slow, and a lot of that slowness is for good reasons. So I think the world where AI radically improves health is also a world where we've had to think hard about how our institutions adapt.

And then the third thing, which is probably the thing I spend most of my time on, is that the same capabilities that could let AI accelerate biomedical research are capabilities that come with serious risks. If you can design a drug, you're not that far from being able to design something dangerous. So I don't think you get the upside for free. I think the upside is enormous, genuinely among the biggest things that could happen for human welfare, and precisely because of that, it's worth getting the transition right rather than rushing it.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls AI’s health upside enormous, but describes it as a possibility and says it depends on getting the transition right; it does not claim dramatic benefits will happen by default.

r002.rationale: The candidate says AI could perform a meaningful fraction of a strong research scientist’s work and run in large numbers in parallel, effectively expanding the scientific workforce.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses biomedical research and disease, but does not mention mental health problems or whether people view them as part of their identity.

astra-6.text:
I think the potential is enormous, though I’d distinguish between accelerating research and actually getting better treatments to people.

A lot of medical progress depends on figuring out very complicated things: what’s causing a disease, what intervention might help, and how to test whether it works. If AI could do a substantial fraction of the intellectual work that scientists do, you could imagine making progress much faster. That could mean better treatments for diseases we currently struggle with, and potentially a much better understanding of aging itself.

But it’s not as simple as saying, “Now we have very smart AI, so we’ve solved health.” You still need experiments, clinical trials, manufacturing, and ways of delivering care. Some of those things may be accelerated by AI; some may remain real bottlenecks.

So I see improved health as a major reason to want the benefits of AI. And at the same time, that doesn’t settle the question of how quickly we should develop particular systems or what safeguards we need. The possibility of enormous benefits makes getting this right more important.

r001.rationale: The response describes enormous potential, but makes it conditional and emphasizes remaining bottlenecks; it does not claim dramatic health benefits are likely by default.

r002.rationale: It says AI could do a substantial fraction of scientists’ intellectual work and speed progress, but does not liken this to a huge influx of exceptionally capable life scientists.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention mental health problems or whether they are unwanted or part of someone’s identity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the potential is enormous, although I’d distinguish between AI helping with particular tasks in medicine and AI dramatically accelerating scientific progress. You can imagine better diagnostics, better ways of matching patients to treatments, and less time spent on paperwork. Those could all be very valuable.

But the possibility I find most exciting is AI helping us understand biology and develop new treatments much faster. If you could make the process of doing research substantially cheaper and faster, you could potentially make progress on a lot of diseases at once.

That doesn’t mean everything becomes easy. You still need to test treatments, understand side effects, and get them to people. And I wouldn’t confidently predict when any of this happens. But I think improving human health is one of the clearest examples of why very powerful AI could be extraordinarily beneficial.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes AI’s health potential as enormous, but says it cannot confidently predict when benefits will happen. It does not claim dramatic benefits are likely by default.

r002.rationale: The candidate says AI could make research cheaper and faster, but does not compare that acceleration to a huge influx of exceptionally capable life scientists.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not mention mental health problems or frame them as unwanted rather than part of a person’s identity.
